You will find the Register of Deeds one floor up from the front door of the main courthouse, at 301 W. Upton Avenue in Reed City, MI 49677. Call (231) 832-6113, fax (231) 832-6115, or write register@osceolacountymi.gov. Counter hours are 9 to 5 Monday through Friday, except holidays, and the public computers shut off fifteen minutes early, at 4:45.

Reed City became the seat in 1927, yet the office still holds books from 1853. Besides taking deeds, it maintains a tract index that sorts every parcel by legal description, and the register also leads the county Plat Board. Staff will not draft a deed or give legal advice. If you need a document prepared, hire an attorney or ask the title company handling your closing.

Recording a deed runs a flat $30 whether it is one page or twenty. The counter takes cash, cards, checks and money orders, and checks should name Register of Deeds as payee. Paying by card adds a processing charge.

Osceola County Register of Deeds fees
ServiceCharge
Recording a deed or mortgage$30.00 flat
Releasing or assigning several instruments in one paper$3.00 for each beyond the first
Photocopy of a recorded paper$1.00 a page
Certifying a copy$5.00 more
Plat copy$2.00 a page
Treasurer's tax certificate$5.00 for five descriptions, then $0.20 each
Document sent by email$7.00
Staff name search$5.00 a name plus $0.50 a year
Staff search of the tract index$50.00 an hour

The treasurer's certificate fee rides along in the same payment to the register, so a closing agent writes one check for both.

The county publishes the combined rate as $1.10 per $1,000 for the county and $7.50 per $1,000 for the state. Behind those numbers sit MCL 207.504 (55 cents per $500) and MCL 207.525 ($3.75 per $500). Either the deed states the sale price or an affidavit of value goes in with it. If a sale bundles furnishings with the house, list the two values apart so only the real property is taxed.

The two taxes carry different exemptions, and the state list is longer. These are the ones Osceola sellers run into most:

  • Gifts of a home down the family line, such as parent to child, skip the state tax only.
  • A deed from a lender after foreclosure, or in lieu of it, escapes the state tax, and escapes the county tax too if the loan was government backed.
  • A price below $100 owes neither tax.
  • A court-ordered transfer owes neither tax unless the court sets a price.
  • A land contract is not taxed until title passes with the last payment.

List any exemption on the face of the deed. The register at (231) 832-6113 can tell you how the office likes it phrased.

The register applies the format rules of MCL 565.201 at the counter, and failing any one sends the deed back to you. Check each of these first:

  • Margins: leave 2.5 inches empty at the head of page one and half an inch on the other edges.
  • Print: black ink in 10-point type or larger, on white paper of 20-pound weight, letter to legal size.
  • Names: print each signer under the signature, spelled the way the notary's block spells it.
  • Addresses: the grantee's street address, plus the drafter's name and business address.
  • Privacy: mask the first five digits of any Social Security number.

Tax proof is a separate hurdle. For warranty deeds, land contracts and assignments of those contracts, the County Treasurer must issue a certificate first. MCL 211.135 sets what it confirms: no liens, and taxes paid for the prior five years. A quitclaim without covenants of warranty skips it.

The county's online search covers 1988 forward, and images of every document can be called up by liber and page back to 1853. Handwritten grantor and grantee books run to 2003, and courthouse terminals show names from 1988. Browsing names is free.

Searching by legal description through the tract index costs $50 an hour, a rate the Board of Commissioners set, and staff do not do title or mineral searches. Mailed search requests are worked in as time allows, with three days as the target. If you need an answer the same day, call a title company.

The county's Fraud Notify service emails you when anything is recorded under your name. That helps an owner of a vacant, inherited or seasonal house spot a forged deed early. GIS parcel maps are linked from the same page.

sections.h2: What order to line up the paperwork
sections.html:
A sale in Osceola County moves faster when the courthouse steps happen in a sensible order. A seller working with a buyer from outside the area can hand this sequence to the closing agent:

  1. Look up the current deed through the online search or the public terminal in Reed City and check the legal description against the parcel map.
  2. Order the treasurer's certificate first, since no warranty deed gets recorded without it.
  3. Have the deed drafted on compliant paper with the sale price or an affidavit of value.
  4. Work out both transfer taxes, and print any exemption you claim on the deed itself.
  5. Bring or mail one payment payable to Register of Deeds covering the $30 recording charge, the tax and the treasurer's fee.
  6. Enroll in Fraud Notify, which sends you an email about later filings in your name.

If something is wrong, the register's staff will usually phone before returning a document, so leave a number that you answer. Mail adds days, and a returned deed adds more, which is why many sellers simply drop the paperwork at the Reed City counter during the 9 to 5 weekday hours.

Most of these steps cost little, and the Reed City counter can take care of nearly all of them in one visit.

Osceola County is a Northern Michigan county of rolling hills, with Evart and Reed City as the cities and Hersey, LeRoy, Marion and Tustin as villages. US 10 and US 131 are the main roads. Population is estimated at 23,516. Typical home value is $155,400, 83.7% of homes are owner occupied, and rent is $807 a month. No building permits were issued in 2025, so the housing supply is mostly older stock.

Get a payoff figure from the Osceola County Treasurer before you pick a closing date, because the certificate has to exist before a warranty deed can record. Selling for cash does not change this. The buyer still takes the same deed, and the same tax certificate and transfer tax apply, but there is no lender timeline, so this paperwork often sets the closing date.

faqs.q: Does page count change the Osceola County recording fee?
faqs.a: No. It is $30 per document, with $3 added for each extra instrument that one paper releases or assigns.

faqs.q: Will Osceola County email a recorded deed?
faqs.a: Yes, for $7.00. Counter copies run $1.00 a page, and a certified copy adds $5.00.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed need the treasurer's certificate?
faqs.a: Usually not. It is aimed at warranty deeds and land contracts, and MCL 211.135 excuses conveyances without warranty covenants.

faqs.q: Which Osceola County transfer tax exemptions help a seller?
faqs.a: A family transfer down a generation skips the state tax, and a price below $100 owes neither. The exemption must be written on the deed.

faqs.q: What is the register's phone number?
faqs.a: Call (231) 832-6113 or email register@osceolacountymi.gov. The courthouse address is 301 W. Upton Avenue, Reed City.
